method: OPEN AND QUOTED from British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y) 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas' (published 11 May 2024). Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: CC BY 4.0 (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> element for PMC11724041).

claims.claim: **The usual presentation is a painless, growing soft tissue lump**; deep tumours are easily missed, and median size at diagnosis is still over 9 cm.
claims.source_text: The most common presentation of a sarcoma is a painless enlarging soft tissue mass. The clinical recognition especially if deep-seated (i.e. thigh, retroperitoneum) can be problematic and the median size at diagnosis remains large, at over 9 cm
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Unexplained lump that is getting bigger: consider urgent ultrasound within 2 weeks.** Refer on a suspected-cancer pathway (seen within 2 weeks) if ultrasound suggests sarcoma, or is uncertain and concern persists.
claims.source_text: Consider an urgent direct access ultrasound scan (to be performed within 2 weeks) to assess for soft tissue sarcoma in adults with an unexplained lump that is increasing in size. Consider a suspected cancer pathway referral (for an appointment within 2 weeks) for adults if they have ultrasound findings that are suggestive of soft tissue sarcoma or if ultrasound findings are uncertain and clinical concern persists.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Any retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal mass that looks like sarcoma on CT or MRI** goes to a specialist sarcoma MDT before anyone operates.
claims.source_text: Any retroperitoneal or intra-abdominal mass with imaging appearances on CT or MRI suggestive of a soft tissue sarcoma should be referred to a specialist sarcoma MDT before surgical treatment.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Diagnose by percutaneous core needle biopsy with several cores**, planned so the tract can be excised at definitive surgery. FNA is not a primary diagnostic test.
claims.source_text: The standard approach to establish a histopathological diagnosis of a suspicious soft tissue mass is by percutaneous core needle biopsy. Multiple cores should be taken to maximise diagnostic yield. … The biopsy should be planned in such a way that the biopsy tract can be safely removed at the time of definitive surgery. … Fine needle aspiration is not recommended as a primary diagnostic modality
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Small subcutaneous lesions under 2 cm that are indeterminate on imaging** can simply be excised, as most prove benign.
claims.source_text: A planned excision biopsy with minimal or no surgical margins may be the most practical option for small subcutaneous lesions that are indeterminate on imaging (<2 cm diameter), as such lesions usually prove to be benign.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Stage most confirmed sarcomas, and all intermediate- or high-grade ones, with CT chest**; add abdomen and pelvis, especially for myxoid liposarcoma, leiomyosarcoma and high-grade lower-limb tumours.
claims.source_text: However, most patients with a confirmed STS, and all those with intermediate and high-grade tumours, should be staged with a CT chest to exclude pulmonary metastases prior to definitive treatment. Though isolated visceral metastases from most sarcomas are uncommon [], at initial staging inclusion of abdomen and pelvis in the CT is usually performed, especially for myxoid liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma, and for high-grade sarcomas of the lower extremities.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After an unplanned excision with positive margins**, stage fully and MRI the surgical bed; re-excise if clear margins are achievable with acceptable morbidity.
claims.source_text: Patients who have undergone inadvertent surgery without a preoperative diagnosis of sarcoma resulting in unplanned positive margins should be fully staged and undergo an MRI of the surgical bed to look for gross residual disease. In the absence of any gross residual disease re-excision of the surgical bed may be advised, if adequate margins can be achieved with acceptable morbidity.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **All decisions on surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and their timing belong to a formal sarcoma MDT.**
claims.source_text: All patients should have their care managed by a formally constituted sarcoma MDT. Decisions about surgery, chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and the timing of all these modalities should be made by the Sarcoma MDT.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Surgery is the standard for localised disease:** en bloc excision with tumour-free margins, preserving function, by a sarcoma-trained surgeon, mostly in a sarcoma centre.
claims.source_text: Surgery is the standard treatment for all patients with an adult-type, localised soft-tissue sarcoma. It must be carried out by a surgeon specifically trained in the treatment of this disease and performed mostly within a sarcoma treatment centre. The standard surgical procedure is an en bloc excision with tumour free margins. This implies removing the tumour in a single specimen with a rim of normal tissue around it, while preserving limb function as best possible.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Radiotherapy, before or after surgery, is standard for most intermediate- or high-grade tumours.** It can be omitted after complete resection of a low-grade tumour, or wide excision of a small superficial high-grade one.
claims.source_text: Both pre- or post-operative radiotherapy are considered standard approaches for most intermediate or high-grade soft tissue sarcomas [], although in the UK pre-operative radiotherapy is more often employed. … Radiotherapy may be avoided in patients with low-grade tumours that have been completely resected, or those with small, superficial high-grade tumours resected with wide margins.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pre- versus post-operative radiotherapy:** local control is the same; pre-operative treatment causes more acute wound complications, post-operative treatment more late toxicity.
claims.source_text: Local control is similar for both pre- and post-operative radiotherapy []. However, risks of acute and late toxicities differ, with preoperative radiotherapy being associated with increased acute, post-operative complications compared to the standard post-operative treatment [], and post-operative radiotherapy being associated with increased late toxicity compared with pre-operative radiotherapy
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Radiotherapy doses:** 60-66 Gy post-operatively, or 50-50.4 Gy pre-operatively, in 1.8-2 Gy fractions, with surgery about 4-8 weeks after pre-operative radiotherapy. Hypofractionated 25-30 Gy in five fractions pre-operatively looks equally effective.
claims.source_text: The recommended dose for post-operative radiotherapy is 60-66 Gy in 1.8-2 Gy fractions, and for pre-operative radiotherapy is 50-50.4 Gy Gy in 1.8-2 Gy fractions []. Timing of surgery is ~4-8 weeks after completion of radiotherapy. Existing evidence does not supporting the role for a post-operative boost if resection margins are positive, as this is unlikely to be beneficial and may result in excess late toxicity [, ]. In recent years, there has been increasing interest in short course hypo-fractionated schedules for pre-operative radiotherapy delivering 25-30 Gy in five fractions over one week, which appear to achieve equivalent local control rates to longer fractionation schedules, without increased toxicity
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Peri-operative chemotherapy is for high-risk and chemo-sensitive disease.** Extremity or trunk sarcomas with predicted 10-year OS under 51% roughly halved their risk of recurrence or death with adjuvant chemotherapy (HR 0.46).
claims.source_text: It may be considered for patients with higher-risk tumours, and potentially more chemo-sensitive subtypes, such as myxoid round cell sarcoma, synovial sarcoma, uterine leiomyosarcoma, and desmoplastic small round cell tumour (DSRCT). … Those patients with extremity or trunk-wall sarcoma and a predicted 10-year OS of less than 51% did benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy, with a halving in the risk of recurrence or death (HR 0.46)
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Neoadjuvant anthracycline plus ifosfamide:** in high-risk patients (predicted 5-year survival under 60%), 3 cycles gave 5-year OS of 0.66 versus 0.55 for histotype-tailored chemotherapy. No trial has compared neoadjuvant chemotherapy with immediate surgery.
claims.source_text: High-risk patients were those with predicted 5-year survival of <60%. A survival advantage was demonstrated for 3 cycles of AI compared with HT therapy in high-risk patients, with a 5-year OS of 0.66 in the AI arm, compared with 0.55 for HT. … It is important to note that, to date, no randomised trial has tested the superiority of neoadjuvant CT vs immediate surgery in operable patients.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Each visit:** history, examination for local recurrence (MRI or CT if suspicious or hard to examine), chest X-ray (CT if abnormal), and checks for late effects.
claims.source_text: It is recommended that standard follow-up consists of: I. clinical history, II. clinical examination to focus on local recurrence, with imaging MRI or CT when indicated by clinical suspicion, or if the primary site is difficult to examine clinically (e.g. intra-abdominal tumours, or deep-seated tumours beneath a flap), III. chest X-ray, with subsequent CT chest used for investigating radiographic abnormalities. IV. Monitoring for late effects of treatment.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Intermediate or high grade:** every 3-4 months for the first 2-3 years, twice yearly to year 5, then yearly for at least 8 to 10 years. **Low grade:** every 6 months for 5 years, then yearly for at least 10 years.
claims.source_text: it is recommended that patients with intermediate/high grade tumours, which most commonly relapse within 2-3 years, should be followed every 3-4 months in the first 2-3 years, then twice a year up to the fifth year, and once a year thereafter for a minimum of 8 to 10 years. It is recommended that patients with low-grade tumours should be followed up every 6 months for 5 years, then annually thereafter, for at least 10 years.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treatment of metastatic disease is almost always palliative.** About 50% of high-grade sarcomas metastasise; median survival from metastasis is about 12 months, perhaps nearer 18 in recent data.
claims.source_text: In almost all cases, the treatment intention for metastatic disease is palliation. Approximately 50% of patients with high-grade sarcoma develop distant metastases and eventually die of disseminated disease, with a median survival of approximately 12 months from diagnosis of metastases [-]. There are more recent data suggesting that this survival figure may be rather conservative with some improvement in outcomes over time to a median of around 18 months
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **First line: doxorubicin alone, or doxorubicin with ifosfamide.** The combination gives more response and PFS but no survival gain and more toxicity, so it suits patients who need shrinkage. For leiomyosarcoma, doxorubicin with dacarbazine is an option.
claims.source_text: In most cases of metastatic soft-tissue sarcoma the choice of first-line chemotherapy will be between single-agent doxorubicin, or combined doxorubicin and ifosfamide. In a European trial a dose-intense ifosfamide/doxorubicin combination did not improve survival, but did deliver a higher response rate and improved progression-free survival, though at the cost of increased toxicity []. This may be an important consideration if the patient is symptomatic due to tumour size, or a reduction in tumour volume might facilitate other treatment options. … An option in locally advanced, or metastatic leiomyosarcoma where a higher response rate is desired, is the combination of doxorubicin and dacarbazine
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Second line: ifosfamide 9-10 g/m2** (monitor closely for renal toxicity), or gemcitabine with docetaxel.
claims.source_text: Standard second-line treatment is ifosfamide, which is also used first-line where anthracyclines are contraindicated, for example in patients at high risk of cardiac complications, or patients pre-treated with anthracyclines. Clinical trials have indicated a dose-response relationship, and a dose of 9-10 g/m2 is recommended … Renal toxicity of ifosfamide can be significant and close monitoring is required. … An alternative second-line option is the combination of gemcitabine and docetaxel.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Trabectedin** is a second-line option, beating dacarbazine in leiomyosarcoma and liposarcoma; myxoid liposarcoma is especially sensitive. Stabilisation may come well before response, and it continues to progression. ⚠️ Watch for rhabdomyolysis and liver toxicity.
claims.source_text: Trabectedin, licensed as second-line treatment for all soft tissue sarcomas, was approved by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) on the basis of a randomised trial comparing two different treatment regimens in patients with predominantly leiomyosarcoma and liposarcoma []. A trial in patients with leiomyosarcoma and liposarcoma comparing trabectedin with dacarbazine demonstrated significant superiority for trabectedin resulting in the drug being licensed in the USA []. Other tumours, such as synovial sarcoma, and particularly myxoid liposarcoma, may also be sensitive. It appears to be active in sarcomas related to chromosomal translocations [, ]. When assessing clinical benefit, it should be noted that a period of disease stabilisation may often occur for some time before response is seen. Trabectedin is currently approved by NICE and treatment can continue until disease progression. It exhibits less haematological toxicity than doxorubicin or ifosfamide, but prescribers need to be aware of rare, but potentially serious rhabdomyolysis, and hepatic toxicity.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Eribulin** is authorised for unresectable liposarcoma after anthracycline treatment; data in other subtypes are limited.
claims.source_text: Eribulin: received marketing authorisation from the EMA in 2016 for the treatment of unresectable liposarcoma following prior anthracycline-containing therapy. This followed subgroup analysis of a study comparing eribulin with dacarbazine for previously treated patients with liposarcoma or leiomyosarcoma []. The data in other sarcoma types is limited [] and it is not currently funded in England for use in sarcomas.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pazopanib** has evidence in metastatic STS other than liposarcoma, improving PFS by 3 months over placebo, with no subtype standing out.
claims.source_text: Pazopanib: Has data supporting its use in metastatic STS (not liposarcoma). A placebo-controlled study demonstrated a 3-month improvement in progression-free survival in STS, with no particular superiority in any individual subtype
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Lung metastases:** base metastasectomy on disease-free interval, other disease, number and growth. Without a meaningful disease-free interval, rescan at three months and operate if no new lesions appear.
claims.source_text: The decision regarding metastasectomy should be based on disease-free period following primary surgery, absence of other metastases, number of lesions per lung, tumour growth, and evolution of disease []. In the absence of a significant disease-free interval, the CT scan (or PET-CT scan to complete staging) should be repeated at a three-month interval, and if no new lesions have appeared and the disease is operable, surgery is usually recommended.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Poor performance status or major comorbidity:** symptom control alone is often best; involve community palliative care early in all advanced disease.
claims.source_text: For a number of patients, particularly those with poor performance status or significant comorbidities, standard supportive care with symptom control alone, is often the most appropriate option. Early involvement of community palliative care teams should be considered in all patients with advanced disease.
claims.locator: British Sarcoma Group, British Journal of Cancer (doi 10.1038/s41416-024-02674-y), 'UK guidelines for the management of soft tissue sarcomas', published 11 May 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11724041/, retrieved 2026-09-23
